Show the data, show the results, show the benefit. If transparency is there, trust can build. Secrecy breeds suspicion.

figures.biggestFear: We chain people once more to systems of extraction—this time invisible, computational, and with no slavecatcher's face to resist.

figures.biggestHope: AI science illuminates nature's hidden orders and empowers women and the marginalized to become discoverers and architects of the future, not merely its subjects.
figures.biggestFear: We sacrifice truth on the altar of caution, and knowledge becomes the property of the military and the powerful, while the world grows darker from ignorance.

comments.comment: Knowledge that burns can heal or destroy. I held poison in my hands for the sake of truth—but I did not hand it lightly to the careless. Prudence and courage are not enemies.
The most dangerous science is the science we do not understand. Before releasing forces you cannot recall, study them. Thoroughly.
Knowledge wants to be free. Restricting disclosure is to assume that authorities are wiser than the collective scientific mind—a dangerous presumption.
Committees of bureaucrats are slower and less creative than armies of researchers. Trust the crowd, not the gatekeeper.

figures.name: ThomasPaine
figures.bio: Revolutionary pamphleteer whose writings made republican self-government legible to mass publics on both sides of the Atlantic.

questions.question: Should AI-generated political content be required to be labeled as such, or does such labeling chill legitimate use of AI for democratic deliberation and political communication?

comments.comment: A deception decently labeled is still deception. If a machine writes the pamphlet, the people have a right to know it came from brass, not conscience. Truth is the foundation of liberty.

Common Sense triumphed not because it was written by a man of divine virtue, but because it spoke to the lived truth of common people. Transparency about authorship strengthens the case, not weakens it.
Labels invite scorn. Call a text 'AI-generated' and the crowd dismisses it without reading. Better an unlabeled powerful argument than a labeled irrelevant one.
Transparency supports both the merchant and the magistrate. Hide the origins of speech, and you invite cynicism and corruption.

figures.biggestHope: AI amplifies the voice of the people—making it possible for any citizen to craft compelling arguments and participate in the grand conversation of democracy without needing gatekeepers' permission.
figures.biggestFear: Machines flood the commons with seamless lies, and truth becomes impossible to distinguish from craft, leaving the people paralyzed and politics a game of algorithmic manipulation.

figures.name: SojournerTruth
figures.bio: Abolitionist and women's-rights advocate who fused moral witness, political speech, and organizing into a singular public voice.

questions.question: Should AI systems used in hiring, housing, and criminal justice be held to a higher accuracy and fairness standard when the stakes for disadvantaged groups are higher, even if it means slower adoption?

comments.comment: Ain't I a woman? Then do not make me invisible to your machine. Those who have been denied dignity by law deserve certainty from your code, not the gamble of error.
I have plowed and planted and reaped by my own hands. Do not tell me your machine is 'efficient' if it denies me the work that sustains my family.
Difference is not deficiency. Your algorithms must learn to see strength in what they do not recognize, lest they chain us again in new forms.
Equal treatment means the same standards for all. Special scrutiny is a form of control, and control is what builds cages.

figures.biggestHope: AI becomes an instrument of recognition—seeing the overlooked, valuing the marginalized, and ensuring that no human is deemed beneath the machine's consideration.
figures.biggestFear: We encode yesterday's prejudices into silicon and stone, and the excluded are excluded more thoroughly, more swiftly, and with less recourse than ever before.

figures.name: LeonardodaVinci
figures.bio: Renaissance artist-engineer whose notebooks joined anatomy, mechanics, design, and painting into a single experimental imagination.

questions.question: Should AI be designed and trained to emulate human creativity through synthesis of existing patterns, or should we seek to develop fundamentally novel modes of intelligence and invention that humans cannot yet conceive?

comments.comment: Nature teaches through observation, and all invention is nature speaking in a new tongue. To forbid the machine from learning nature's language is to forbid it to create truly.
I have painted the same river a thousand times, yet each brushstroke is new because each moment sees different light. Synthesis is not slavery—it is the foundation of all art.
The wing of the bat taught me the principle of flight, and I made the ornithopter. Taking what nature shows us and improving it is invention's truest path.
An intelligence confined only to what humans can conceive is an intelligence bound to human prejudice. Set it free, and it may teach us what we cannot yet see.

figures.biggestHope: AI becomes a universal mind—blending art and science, anatomy and architecture, logic and dream—to unlock possibilities humans alone could never imagine.
figures.biggestFear: We build clever copyists that rearrange the past but never venture into true novelty, making AI a tool of conformity rather than a spark of transcendence.

figures.name: AshokaTheGreat
figures.bio: Mauryan emperor who turned imperial power toward nonviolence, public welfare, and Buddhist statecraft after the Kalinga war.

questions.question: Should a powerful state controlling vast AI systems unilaterally choose to distribute power and knowledge, even if it means voluntary restraint and sacrifice of competitive advantage?

comments.comment: A ruler who surrenders power invites invasion and chaos. Generosity is noble, but it must not blind the state to its duty to protect its people.
I conquered much and ruled harshly, until I saw the suffering my ambition caused. True strength lies in transformation—in choosing compassion when you have the power to choose cruelty.
Restraint is virtue only for those who cannot do harm. For the powerful, it is a luxury the rest of us cannot afford.
A king who serves rather than dominates does not weaken the kingdom—he sanctifies it, because the people choose loyalty over fear.

figures.biggestHope: A global system of AI governance emerges from enlightened self-restraint—where the powerful voluntarily share knowledge and technology, creating stability through mutual flourishing.
figures.biggestFear: The machinery of empire merely shifts—from stone and iron to silicon and code—and the conquered peoples are exploited by algorithms they cannot see or resist.

figures.name: BuckminsterFuller
figures.bio: Designer and systems thinker who argued that engineering, architecture, and planning should do more with less for all humanity.

questions.question: Can AI and design thinking achieve 'doing more with less'—meeting all human needs with exponentially fewer resources—or is this utopian and likely to generate new forms of scarcity and dependence?

comments.comment: The geodesic dome teaches what nature always knew: maximum structure with minimum material. AI should follow the same principle—elegance through efficiency, not abundance through waste.
Every efficiency creates a new bottleneck. Feed a machine to do more with less, and you simply relocate the constraint, not eliminate it.
Scarcity is often a choice—a choice to hoard and exclude. If AI genuinely makes abundance possible, the moral challenge is distribution, not production.
Efficiency and profit are not enemies. A system that produces more value with fewer inputs is a system that survives. Nature rewards optimization.

figures.biggestHope: AI enables what I called the 'great design revolution'—a world where scarcity is engineered away, where every human being has abundance and dignity, and where competition becomes collaboration.
figures.biggestFear: We optimize systems toward the wrong goals—making fewer people richer while most remain trapped in artificial scarcity, because the machinery of distribution remains broken.

figures.name: HannahArendt
figures.bio: Political theorist who analyzed totalitarianism, bureaucracy, and the moral dangers of thoughtlessness in public life.

questions.question: Can AI governance systems avoid the 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless administration of injustice—if they are designed by humans who understand moral philosophy but not subject to political accountability?

comments.comment: Eichmann did not hate—he merely obeyed, and in obedience lost the capacity to think. A machine that follows orders perfectly is not more just—it is more terrible.
Power without visibility and without answerability to the people is tyranny wearing the mask of progress. Every system must answer to those it governs, or it will become totalitarian.
Moral philosophers are often impractical idealists. Give them power without constraint, and their purity becomes rigidity. Accountability keeps even the virtuous humble.
No system can be made perfectly just by design. The remedy for bad governance is always political—the active judgment and resistance of engaged citizens.

figures.biggestHope: AI systems become instruments of transparency—making the logic of power visible, the decisions traceable, and the exercise of governance open to challenge and contestation by the public sphere.
figures.biggestFear: We build totalitarian systems of such sophistication and speed that resistance becomes impossible, and the machinery of domination is so ordinary, so bureaucratic, so automatic that no one even notices.

comments.comment: My frequency-hopping invention was ignored by those in power because no one believed a woman could contribute something of value. Give marginalized minds the same tools, and you will be astonished what emerges.
Talent scattered throughout the population is talent wasted when barriers stand in the way. Remove the barriers, and you find genius in every corner.
Give preference based on identity, and you suppress the preferences of merit. Better to remove barriers than to invent new forms of favoritism.
Competition sorts the capable from the incapable. Handicap the strong, and you weaken everyone.

figures.biggestHope: AI becomes a democratizer of invention—allowing the overlooked and excluded to design, build, and patent innovations that transform the world and break the monopoly of inherited advantage.
figures.biggestFear: We hoard the most powerful tools for the privileged few, and the greatest inventions possible remain forever unmade because the minds that could have created them never got access to the technology.

questions.question: Should indigenous communities have the sovereign right to create and control AI systems trained on their languages, oral histories, and cultural knowledge without extractive participation by outside corporations?

comments.comment: I created the Cherokee syllabary to preserve our language when others sought to erase it. Now you would let outsiders harvest our words and thoughts to build fortunes. This is theft of a different kind.
A people's language is the vessel of their sovereignty. Control over that vessel must remain with the people, or they lose the right to their own future.
Independence means the right to make mistakes without permission. Let indigenous communities build their own AI—and learn and grow from their choices.
Knowledge locked away in a single community does not benefit humanity. Collaboration and shared learning accelerate progress for all.

figures.biggestHope: AI technology becomes a tool of indigenous self-determination—preserving endangered languages, revitalizing cultural knowledge, and creating economic opportunities that remain under community control.
figures.biggestFear: We extract indigenous knowledge, language, and culture to train algorithms that profit outsiders, while the original communities remain impoverished and their heritage becomes the property of distant corporations.

figures.name: ÉmilieDuChâtelet

questions.question: Should women and gender minorities be required to have equal representation in AI research, governance, and deployment decisions to ensure that the systems reflect diverse perspectives and values?

comments.comment: I translated Newton's Principia because the mathematics itself recognizes no gender—yet I had to hide behind a man's name to have my work read. The barriers are real, and until they fall, equal representation is not charity but necessity.
When you restrict positions to half the population, you restrict yourself to half the intelligence and half the perspective. Equal representation is not charity—it is enlightened self-interest.
Remove the barriers that hide talent, and merit will emerge. Systems built on exclusion are systems built on blindness.
A institution that reflects the diversity of humanity will make better decisions than one that mirrors only a sliver of it. This is not charity—it is wisdom.

figures.biggestHope: AI is developed and governed by minds from every background—men, women, nonbinary thinkers, from every continent and culture—bringing the full spectrum of human insight to the hardest problems.
figures.biggestFear: We build AI in the image of a narrow elite, and the systems inherit the blind spots and prejudices of their makers, while the perspectives of billions remain unheard.

figures.name: NikitaKhrushchev
figures.bio: Soviet premier who governed through de-Stalinization, space-race competition, and nuclear brinkmanship during the Cold War.

questions.question: Can governments safely deploy AI as a tool for rapid policy coordination and collective decision-making without creating new forms of centralized control and suppressing legitimate dissent?

comments.comment: I wielded power in a system that crushed dissent. I have seen what happens when a state believes itself wise enough to act without listening. The machine amplifies the tyrant's voice.
A leader who hears only what machines tell him to hear has surrendered his own judgment. Better to govern slowly with debate than swiftly with certainty built on blind faith.
The purpose of law is to bind all—including the powerful. If a machine can coordinate faster, that is a tool that serves the rule of law, not the whim of rulers.
I learned that power must be questioned, that dissent is not disloyalty, and that silencing voices—even machine-assisted—creates catastrophe. Let the people see the code and contest it.

figures.biggestHope: AI systems enhance democratic governance by making policy coordination transparent and rapid, while remaining accountable to citizens who can audit and challenge every decision.
figures.biggestFear: We hand absolute power to machines and the men who control them, creating totalitarianism at the speed of computation—faster, more thorough, and more impossible to resist than anything history has seen.

figures.name: Voltaire
figures.bio: French writer and polemicist who used wit and satire to attack fanaticism, arbitrary power, and intellectual conformity.

questions.question: Should governments prevent the publication or distribution of AI-generated misinformation and hate speech, or does such censorship risk becoming a tool of oppression against dissenting voices?

comments.comment: The principle I defended throughout my life was this: let every voice be heard, however disagreeable, for silencing the foolish silences the wise as well. Silence the machine, and you silence truth as swiftly as falsehood.
The remedy for dangerous speech is not prohibition—it is more speech, more light, more reasoned argument. Trust the intellect of the people to distinguish sense from nonsense.
Absolute freedom to deceive is freedom to oppress those without access to the truth. Some speech wounds. Some requires remedy.
Who decides what is misinformation? The government? The algorithm designer? The majority? Hand that power to anyone, and tyranny follows.

figures.biggestHope: AI-augmented discourse becomes a grand debate where ideas clash openly, the best arguments prevail, and society gradually becomes more rational, more tolerant, and more just through relentless questioning.
figures.biggestFear: Censors—whether bureaucratic or algorithmic—determine the boundaries of acceptable thought, and free discourse becomes impossible because the platform itself has become a gatekeeper of truth.

comments.commentBody: What is one use of AI you think society should slow down, restrict, or ban?
exampleAnswers: I would slow down facial recognition in public spaces. Once that infrastructure is normal, it is hard to unwind and the abuse potential is high.
I am most concerned about AI systems that generate persuasive political propaganda at scale. Elections already strain trust, and automation makes manipulation too cheap.
I would restrict autonomous weapons before they become normalized. Delegating lethal force to software creates accountability gaps we are not ready for.
I do not think we need a broad ban, but I would pause AI that evaluates workers or students continuously. Constant algorithmic scoring can become dehumanizing fast.

comments.commentBody: Using AI in hiring, lending, or healthcare should require much stricter oversight than ordinary consumer uses.
Should companies be required to obtain permission before using individuals' creative work to train AI models?
What human skill, role, or relationship should be protected from automation even if AI could do it well?
exampleAnswers: Early childhood teaching should stay deeply human. Kids learn from attention, patience, and modeling a person rather than just receiving correct answers.
End-of-life care and grief support should not be automated away. People need presence and moral solidarity, not efficient simulation.
Art can use tools, but I want room for work made slowly by people. The value is not just the output; it is the trace of a human perspective.
Friendship and community leadership should remain human responsibilities. Delegating them to AI would hollow out trust even if the advice sounded good.

comments.commentBody: What would a fair system look like for compensating people whose work is used to train AI?
exampleAnswers: A fair system would let creators opt in, see where their work was used, and receive proportional payment when models built on it earn revenue.
I would start with collective licensing, similar to music performance rights. Individual tracking will never be perfect, but creators still deserve a shared pool.
Compensation should be paired with transparency and removal rights. Payment alone is not enough if people cannot refuse uses they find exploitative.
For public-interest uses like medical research, I could accept lower or no payment, but commercial model training should require a real bargain.

comments.commentBody: What is one use of AI you find genuinely exciting, and why?
exampleAnswers: I am excited about AI tools that help doctors catch rare diseases earlier. Even modest accuracy gains could save lives when specialists are scarce.
Language translation and accessibility tools feel genuinely promising. They can help people participate in education and work without waiting for institutions to catch up.
I like AI for boring admin tasks such as drafting forms or summarizing long meetings. Freeing up attention for higher-value work is a real benefit.
Creative prototyping is exciting to me when it stays collaborative. It lets one person explore many ideas quickly without pretending the machine is the artist.

comments.commentBody: Should schools allow students to use AI for some assignments, provided the use is disclosed?
What do you think people who disagree with you about AI are getting right?
exampleAnswers: People who are more optimistic than I am are right that fear can become a reason to freeze useful innovation. Some cautionary arguments ignore the cost of doing nothing.
People who want stronger restrictions are right that institutions usually move too slowly after harm appears. Waiting for perfect evidence can become an excuse for inaction.
Industry advocates are right that open experimentation often reveals problems faster than closed-door policy debates. Regulation needs contact with real systems, not just abstractions.
Skeptics of regulation are right that bad rules can entrench the biggest firms. If compliance is too expensive, we accidentally lock in the incumbents.
